title: Vernacular health misinformation and its negotiation by frontline community health workers (Mkhize, Dlamini & Nkosi, International Journal of Advanced Mass Communication and Journalism 7(6), 2026)
screen_reason: Structured observation of 480 community-health-worker/community-member interactions in four South African provinces, coded by two researchers for the presence of false or misleading health claims. 198/480 (41.3%) contained at least one misinformation encounter - a quantitative share with a denominator, coded against an external (biomedical) standard.

estimates.country: South Africa (Western Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Gauteng, Eastern Cape)
estimates.platform: face-to-face conversation during community health worker home visits (offline, vernacular languages)
estimates.date: February to July 2024 (six months of observation)
estimates.measure_type: % of observed CHW-community member interactions that contained at least one health misinformation encounter
estimates.value_raw: "Of the 480 observed interactions, 198 (41.3%) contained at least one misinformation encounter."
estimates.denominator: 480 structured observations of CHW-community member interactions during routine home visits, from eight community health centres (two per province) and 36 CHWs, February-July 2024
estimates.definition: Observer recorded the presence of at least one false or misleading health claim stated by the community member during the visit, coded with a deductive framework covering six health domains (vaccine safety, HIV/AIDS treatment, maternal health, nutrition and diet, traditional medicine, COVID-19 prevention)
estimates.misinfo_def: "False and misleading health claims circulating in vernacular languages through community networks"
estimates.source_quote: Of the 480 observed interactions, 198 (41.3%) contained at least one misinformation encounter.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 35 (repeated in Discussion, p. 37, and Conclusion, p. 38)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: "Two field researchers coded all observations; inter-rater agreement reached 84.6 per cent (Cohen's kappa = 0.79)"; deductive coding framework derived from the health-misinformation and health-literacy literatures; claims judged against biomedical standards, not against a fact-checker list
estimates.moderator_quote: Structured observations covered 480 CHW-community member interactions, recorded during routine home visits over six months (February to July 2024). Each observation was documented using a standardised field note template capturing the health topic discussed, presence and type of misinformation, the CHW's response strategy, and the community member's reaction.
estimates.notes: Construct is borderline: the unit of the denominator is a face-to-face interaction, not a media item, a person or a piece of consumed content. Coded CONTENT because the denominator is all communication units observed and each was coded for the presence of false/misleading claims; an EXPOSURE reading (41.3% of a CHW's home visits expose her to misinformation) or a REACH-style reading are both defensible. denom_scope 'topical' because the observed universe is health conversations across six health domains. Caution on provenance: the journal and the single-institute authorship give no way to verify the dataset from the text, and the paper reports no province-level or domain-level denominators.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: the domain-level rates ('HIV/AIDS treatment (mean prevalence 55.8 encounters per 100 interactions across provinces)' and 'traditional medicine (45.5 per 100)') - these are encounters per 100 interactions (an intensity rate that can exceed the share of interactions), reported for only two of six domains, with no domain-specific denominators; the full domain-by-province matrix exists only as a heatmap image (Fig 1) that is not machine-readable. Table 1's breakdown of the 198 encounters by misinformation type (efficacy denial 27.3%, conspiracy 19.2%, traditional superiority 15.7%, side-effect exaggeration 14.1%, diet-based cure 12.1%, authority distrust 11.6%) is a within-misinformation typology, not a prevalence share. Table 2 (CHW strategy use and perceived effectiveness, n=36) measures correction strategies, not misinformation prevalence.

rob.design: Mixed-methods: structured observation of 480 CHW-community member interactions over six months (Feb-Jul 2024) in eight purposively selected community health centres across four provinces, with 36 purposively recruited CHWs (nine per province, >=2 years' experience); standardised field-note template; two field researchers coded all observations with 84.6% agreement and Cohen's kappa = 0.79; chi-square tests across provinces; plus 36 interviews and four focus groups. No sampling frame for households, no refusal/decline rate, no per-province denominators, and no published coding manual.
rob.item6_quote: Observation data were coded using a deductive framework derived from the health-misinformation and health-literacy literatures. Six health domains were tracked: vaccine safety, HIV/AIDS treatment, maternal health, nutrition and diet, traditional medicine, and COVID-19 prevention.
rob.item10_quote: Of the 480 observed interactions, 198 (41.3%) contained at least one misinformation encounter.
